turns:
=== CALL C0532 ===
Mark: Hiya mate, can you hear me alright? Mark, from Brierley Hill, near Dudley.
Craig: Yeah, er, I can hear you. I'm Craig. Lowestoft.
Mark: Lowestoft! Right on the coast, ain't it? Never been. Furthest east I've got is Great Yarmouth on a works do, and I don't remember much of that, to be honest with you.
Craig: Ha. Yeah, it's just down the road from Yarmouth. Bit quieter.
Mark: Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was sat there going round in circles, I'll be honest. Julie come in and asked if I was alright 'cause I was swearing at the laptop.
Craig: Erm, yeah. I dunno how I did. Sort of just guessed the last few.
Mark: Same, mate, same. So what do you do with yourself, then?
Craig: Er... nothing at the minute really. I was a welder, fabricator, at an offshore yard. Got laid off last year, then my back went, so.
Mark: Oh, your back, yeah? Join the club. Mine's been knackered three years now. I was on a depot near Merry Hill, picking and loading, and one day it just went, and the knee went with it. Body's done what it can, ain't it. Doctor says to me, Mark, you've got the spine of a seventy year old, and I says, well give it me back then, 'cause I want the one I had! Nah, I'm alright, I get by. Do bits for mates when I can.
Craig: Yeah. Mine's the lower back. Physio give me stretches. I do 'em when I remember.
Mark: When you remember, yeah, that's the trick, ain't it. I've got a sheet of 'em stuck on the fridge, Julie points at it every morning.
Craig: Ha. Yeah. Gemma's the same. My wife. She's a care assistant, works nights a lot.
Mark: No! Julie's in care an' all. Part-time though. Hard work, that. They don't get paid what they should.
Craig: No, they don't. She's sort of carrying everything at the minute, so. Yeah.
Mark: I know how that feels, mate, honestly. First year I was off I felt proper useless. You get used to it. Not saying it's right, but you do. What you looking at doing, then, anything?
Craig: Erm, maybe maintenance, workshop stuff. Or forklift. Something lighter. I dunno really.
Mark: Forklift! I had me licence, let it lapse. Wanna keep yours up, whatever you do, I'm telling you.
Craig: Yeah, my welding tickets have gone and lapsed an' all. Never was good at keeping on top of that side of it.
Mark: Nobody is, mate. Paperwork. Who's got time for it. You got a dog? I can see a mug there, is that Ipswich?
Craig: Yeah, Ipswich. And yeah, Staffy. Dexter. Bit on the chunky side.
Mark: Staffy! I've got a Staffie cross, Roxy. She's down there somewhere snoring. Chunky's alright, they're built like that, ain't they, little barrels.
Craig: Ha, that's him. He's got a dodgy stomach as well, so he's a nightmare if he gets hold of anything. Ate half a sausage roll off the seafront last week, I was up at three with him.
Mark: Oh no. Oh, I've been there. Roxy had a whole bap off my grandson once, ham and all, and the next morning, well, I won't describe it, you might be having your tea. So Ipswich, eh? How they doing?
Craig: Alright, actually. Better than they have been. Been to Portman Road a couple times with my brother-in-law.
Mark: I'm Albion, West Brom, had a season ticket for years. Watch it down the pub now with my lad. It's the moaning I miss, you know, sat with all the same blokes moaning every week.
Craig: Yeah. I watch it on my phone mostly. Bit quiet on your own.
Mark: You wanna get down the pub for it, mate, even with a lemonade. Gets you out the house. That's what saved me, the darts on a Thursday.
Craig: Yeah... fair enough. I've got a motorbike in the yard I'm meant to be doing up, that's sort of my thing.
Mark: You're joking! I've got an old Escort in the garage, been nearly done since about two thousand and nine.
Craig: Ha. Mine's two years. A 125. Watch loads of them restoration videos on YouTube, then go out there and just look at it.
Mark: That's it, that's exactly it, you look at it, you have a cup of tea, you go back in. We should start a club, mate.
Craig: Yeah. Yeah, it's alright, that.

=== CALL C0533 ===
Rayhan: Hi, erm, can you hear me okay?
Aneesa: Yes, I can hear you. Hi. I'm Aneesa.
Rayhan: I'm Rayhan. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from?
Aneesa: Bradford. You?
Rayhan: Ilford, East London. Erm. Did you find that puzzle at the start alright?
Aneesa: It was fine. I was more interested in why they put it first, to be honest. I think it's to put everyone in the same sort of mood before the calls. Or tired. One of the two.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah, I was tired after it. I'd just got in from work as well.
Aneesa: What do you do?
Rayhan: I'm an apprentice electrician, final year. Small firm in Barking, mostly houses: rewires, kitchens, bit of shop fit-out. I've got my AM2 coming up, that's like the final practical assessment, so I'm a bit... yeah. Revising for that.
Aneesa: That sounds quite intense. Is it all practical?
Rayhan: Mostly. You get a set time to install and test a little setup in a booth, and they mark everything. You can't really rush it. If you mess up the testing you're done, basically. I test twice anyway, the lads on site wind me up for it.
Aneesa: Twice seems sensible when it's electricity.
Rayhan: That's what I say! Erm, what about you, what do you do?
Aneesa: I'm doing a psychology degree with the Open University, second year. And I work part-time in a fragrance shop in town, Saturdays mainly.
Rayhan: Oh, nice. So is this sort of your area, then, these studies?
Aneesa: Kind of. I do a few of them. Partly for the money, I won't lie. But I like seeing how they're set up, what they're actually measuring. Like the photo bit earlier, rating people on a picture, that's a first impressions thing. Then they'll compare it with what we say after.
Rayhan: Oh. I didn't really think about that. I just sort of went with my gut.
Aneesa: That's what they want, I think. It's fine.
Rayhan: Yeah. Your photo, the planner on the wall, it reminded me of my sister. She's doing her GCSEs, she's got colours for every subject.
Aneesa: Guilty. Mine's colour-coded too. I've got a sister who's fourteen. She just borrows my eyeliner and ignores the planner entirely.
Rayhan: Ha. Mine's alright, she asks me for maths help. I got a 7 in maths so I'm the go-to.
Aneesa: That's useful. Do you get much time, with the work and revising?
Rayhan: Not loads. I do football Thursday, gym some mornings. Weekends is mostly family stuff, weddings. There's always a wedding.
Aneesa: There's always a wedding. Same here.
Rayhan: Have you been anywhere nice, travelling? I went to Istanbul last summer with two mates, first time without family.
Aneesa: Istanbul? That's the one place I really want to go. I'm learning Turkish on Duolingo, I've got a streak of four hundred and something days. Was it good?
Rayhan: It was really good, yeah. The mosques, like the Blue Mosque and Süleymaniye, the architecture is unbelievable. And the food. I did the whole itinerary in a spreadsheet, my mates took the mick but we saw everything.
Aneesa: You did a spreadsheet? I did that for Barcelona with my cousins. Every hour planned. They complained the whole time and then thanked me after.
Rayhan: Same! That's exactly what happened. Would you use the Turkish, if you went?
Aneesa: I'd try. I can order tea and ask where the toilet is, so I'd survive. I'd mostly want to sit in Süleymaniye and draw the tiles. I do geometric patterns, ink drawings.
Rayhan: Oh, is that the one behind you? The star?
Aneesa: Yeah, that's one of mine.
Rayhan: That's really neat. Like, properly precise. I'd mess that up.
Aneesa: You'd probably be fine. You test everything twice.

=== CALL C0534 ===
Kerry: Hiya! Oh, you're the West Brom shirt. I clocked that in the photos, I was like, he looks like a laugh.
Mark: Ha, guilty, mate. Mark. Brierley Hill. And you're, er, Kerry, is it?
Kerry: Kerry, yeah. Swindon. Don't say anything about the Magic Roundabout, everyone does.
Mark: I wasn't going to! I was, actually. Is it as bad as they say?
Kerry: Honestly, it's fine once you know it. It's the A419 that's the nightmare. I'm on it every day for work and it's just, do you know what I mean, cones for the sake of cones.
Mark: Oh, don't. Round Merry Hill they've had the road up that long, I reckon the cones have got their own postcode. What is it you do, then?
Kerry: Business development for a building and roofing supplier. So trade accounts, contractors, chasing new business across Wiltshire and Gloucestershire. Basically I'm the one who gets the big accounts in. It's a lot of phone, bit of site visits, showroom. I'm good at it, to be fair, I just think they don't pay what it's worth.
Mark: Nobody ever does, do they. Sounds like you can talk, anyway.
Kerry: I can talk, yeah. Did a negotiation skills course last year and the bloke running it said I was a natural. So.
Mark: There you go then. I'd have been rubbish at that, I just chat. I was on a depot, picking and loading, but the back went, so I'm off now. Just had a lad on before you, Craig, same thing, back's gone. We was swapping notes like two old crocks.
Kerry: Oh no. My back's not great either, to be honest, it's why I don't really do the gym. That's my excuse anyway.
Mark: That's a good excuse, I'd keep that one.
Kerry: Ha! I've had three memberships. Dan, my husband, says I just pay them a direct debit to feel guilty.
Mark: Julie says the same about my darts. I'm on the team down the local, Thursdays. She says it's not a sport if you can do it with a pint in your hand.
Kerry: She's not wrong though, is she?
Mark: She is not, no.
Kerry: Have you been watching The Traitors? Everyone at work's obsessed.
Mark: Julie has it on. I sort of half watch it with my tea and then ask who's who and she gets the hump.
Kerry: Oh, I'd get the hump. Last night was unreal. I'd be so good on that, I can read people, it's literally my job. I'd be a traitor, obviously.
Mark: Obviously! I'd be banished first week, me, I can't keep me face straight.
Kerry: You've got an honest face, to be fair.
Mark: That's what the darts lads say before I take their money. Got any kids, Kerry?
Kerry: Erm, no. No. We've got Biscuit, he's a cockapoo, he's basically the kid. He chewed my new trainers last week, sixty quid.
Mark: Oh, they do, don't they. My Roxy's too old to chew now, she just snores. I've got two grown up, and the grandkids. Off to Towyn with them next weekend in the caravan.
Kerry: Aw, Towyn. I couldn't do a caravan, I'm more all-inclusive, Tenerife, Turkey. Went to Dubai a couple of years ago, that was something else.
Mark: Dubai, eh? Bit posh for me, mate. Give me a pint by a pool in Benidorm and I'm happy.
Kerry: Nothing wrong with that. Bit of sun, cocktail, done.
Mark: Exactly, that's all you want, ain't it. Life's too short.
Kerry: It is. That's what I keep telling Dan when he looks at the bank statements.
Mark: Ha! Julie does the statements in our house. I'm not allowed near.
Kerry: Probably for the best, honestly.

=== CALL C0535 ===
Kerry: Hiya! You're the quiet lad with the hi-vis in the wardrobe. I'm Kerry, Swindon.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah, that's me. Rayhan. I'm in Ilford, East London.
Kerry: So are you on a site, then? Building?
Rayhan: Erm, sort of. I'm an apprentice electrician, final year. Mostly houses, rewires, kitchens, extensions. Bit of shop fit-out sometimes.
Kerry: No way! My husband's a sparky. Dan. Self-employed, round Swindon. So I know all about it, believe me. The van takes up the whole drive, there's cable in my kitchen drawers.
Rayhan: Ha, that sounds about right. My boss's van is the same, except it's always on empty.
Kerry: Oh, Dan's is always on empty and all. What is it with electricians? Are you going self-employed, then, when you're done?
Rayhan: Eventually, yeah, I'd like to. I've got my AM2 first, that's the final assessment. Then inspection and testing. Maybe my own van in my mid-twenties, me and a mate.
Kerry: Right. Well, honestly, do it. Dan's doing alright and he's terrible at the business side. Like he's a brilliant electrician, but quotes, invoices, chasing people for money, he's useless. I sort of do all that for him, or I tell him how to word things. That's literally my job, I'm business development for a building and roofing supplier. I sit on the phone and get contractors to open accounts with us. You want someone like me on your side when you go out on your own, do you know what I mean?
Rayhan: Yeah, that makes sense. I'm alright with the paperwork side, I keep my job notes and test sheets neat. It's more like getting customers that worries me.
Kerry: That's the easy bit! You just ring people. Find out who signs off the money and talk to them, not the receptionist. Don't waste your time being nice to the wrong person.
Rayhan: Erm, okay. I'd probably still be nice to the receptionist though.
Kerry: Ha. Fair enough, you're sweet. Where do you get your stuff from, Screwfix?
Rayhan: Mostly, yeah. Or the wholesaler the firm uses. The tool prices at Screwfix are mad, though.
Kerry: See, that's where a trade account comes in. You get the discounts. I do Dan's discounts, he never even asks, he just pays what's on the shelf.
Rayhan: Yeah, my boss has got one. I just use his.
Kerry: Use his while you can, mate. So what do you do when you're not wiring things?
Rayhan: Football Thursday, five-a-side. Gym some mornings. Watch Arsenal. Family stuff at weekends, there's always a wedding or something.
Kerry: Oh, I love a wedding. We had ours near Marlborough, big do at a hotel, honestly better than anyone else's I've been to. Free bar till ten.
Rayhan: That sounds nice.
Kerry: It was. Are you seeing anyone, then? Are they on at you about getting married?
Rayhan: Erm. A bit, yeah. My brother got married last year, so now everyone's looking at me. I'm not ready, I want to qualify first.
Kerry: Good for you. Don't let them rush you. Everyone's always asking me when I'm having kids, I'm like, mind your own.
Rayhan: Yeah. That's it really.
Kerry: Did you do that puzzle at the start? I thought it was a bit pointless, to be honest.
Rayhan: Erm, I didn't mind it. I was tired, I'd just come in from work.
Kerry: Oh, I'm knackered and all, I've been on the phone all day. Right, well, when you get your van, look me up. Swindon's not that far.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah. Thanks. I'll remember that.

=== CALL C0536 ===
Aneesa: Hi. Can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah, er, yeah. Hi. I'm Craig.
Aneesa: Aneesa. I'm in Bradford.
Craig: Lowestoft. Suffolk.
Aneesa: Is that the one right on the coast?
Craig: Yeah. Most easterly bit of the country, so. That's what it's known for really.
Aneesa: Oh, I didn't know that. Do you live near the sea?
Craig: Sort of, yeah. Ten minute walk. I take the dog along the front early, when it's quiet. Gets windy, mind.
Aneesa: That sounds nice, actually. What kind of dog?
Craig: Staffy. Dexter. He's a bit chunky.
Aneesa: We don't have a dog. My brother keeps asking but my mum says no. He's seventeen, he'd never walk it.
Craig: Ha. No, probably not. It's sort of mostly me with Dexter. My wife works shifts.
Aneesa: What do you do?
Craig: Er... nothing at the minute. I was a welder. Offshore yard. Got laid off, then the back went. So I'm looking for something lighter.
Aneesa: Sorry, that sounds difficult.
Craig: Yeah. It's alright. It is what it is. You?
Aneesa: I'm doing a psychology degree, part-time, with the Open University. And I work in a fragrance shop on Saturdays.
Craig: Oh right. Psychology. So you're like, working out what this is all about, then? The study?
Aneesa: Ha, a bit. I can't help it. I think the photo ratings are the main thing, first impressions, and then these calls test whether you change your mind. And the surveys after, obviously.
Craig: Right. I just put whatever, to be honest.
Aneesa: That's fine. That's probably more useful to them than me overthinking it.
Craig: Ha. Yeah.
Aneesa: Is welding hard to learn? I've always wondered. It looks very precise.
Craig: Erm, it's practice really. MIG's easier, stick takes longer to get right. You've got to keep a steady hand and watch your pool, the molten bit. Get the speed wrong and it's all lumpy. I watch loads of videos of people doing it still, rebuilding old trailers and that. Saw one last week, bloke took this trailer that was basically rust and cut it all back, new box section, welded it up lovely. I could watch that all day.
Aneesa: I get that. I draw geometric patterns, ink. It's the same sort of thing, I think, steady hand, and if one line's off the whole thing's off.
Craig: Yeah, that's it. Is that the one behind you?
Aneesa: Yeah.
Craig: That's tidy, that.
Aneesa: Thank you. Do you still do any welding? Just for yourself?
Craig: Not really. I've got a motorbike in the yard, a 125, I'm meant to be doing it up. Been two years.
Aneesa: Two years? What's stopping you?
Craig: Dunno. I just go out and look at it. Bloke I had on earlier, Mark, he's got a car in his garage the same. He said we should start a club.
Aneesa: Ha. You'd need a planner. I'd make you one, colour-coded.
Craig: Ha. Yeah, Gemma'd love that. Yeah, it's alright, actually. Might do a bit this weekend.

=== CALL C0537 ===
Kerry: Hiya! You're Craig, yeah? I'm Kerry, Swindon. You remind me of my husband, by the way, that's a compliment.
Craig: Ha. Er, okay. Thanks. Yeah, Craig. Lowestoft.
Kerry: Lowestoft. Is that Norfolk?
Craig: Suffolk. Just. Yarmouth's Norfolk.
Kerry: Right, sorry, I'm terrible with that side of the country. Never had a reason to go, do you know what I mean? So what do you do?
Craig: Erm. Nothing at the minute. I was a welder. Back went.
Kerry: Oh, you're Mark's mate! He said he had a lad on with a bad back, you were swapping notes.
Craig: Ha. Yeah, that's me. He's a laugh, Mark.
Kerry: He is, isn't he? He was my favourite so far, no offence. My back's bad too, actually. Lower back, comes and goes. I get migraines and all. I keep meaning to go to the GP but you can never get an appointment in Swindon, it's like winning the lottery.
Craig: Yeah. I've got a physio. Took ages to get, mind.
Kerry: See, that's the thing. So what are you going for, then, job-wise?
Craig: Erm, something lighter. Maintenance. Maybe forklift. I dunno really.
Kerry: Honestly, have you thought about sales? Trade sales, like I do. I'm business development for a building supplier. You'd know the products, the contractors would trust you because you've actually done the job. That's half the battle. And there's a bonus.
Craig: Er... I dunno. I'm not really a phone person.
Kerry: Nobody is at first. You just get on with it.
Craig: Yeah. Maybe. Fair enough.
Kerry: Is that your wedding photo behind you?
Craig: Yeah. Gemma. Got married in church, back home.
Kerry: Aw. We did registry office then a massive do at a hotel near Marlborough. Best party of the year, everyone said. Where'd you go on honeymoon?
Craig: Tenerife.
Kerry: Oh, I love Tenerife! Which bit?
Craig: Erm, the south. Can't remember the name. Big hotel, pool.
Kerry: Playa de las Americas, prob. We've done Tenerife twice, Lanzarote, Turkey. Dubai was the best though. Have you been?
Craig: No. Money's a bit tight at the minute, so. Might do a couple of nights somewhere for our anniversary. Norfolk or something.
Kerry: That's nice though. Cosy.
Craig: Yeah. It's alright.
Kerry: Dan's always on at me about money. He's careful, I'm not. He'd get on with you.
Craig: Ha. Gemma does all the money in ours. Probably for the best.
Kerry: That's what Mark said! Everyone's wife does the money. Except me, obviously.
Craig: Ha. Yeah.
Kerry: Have you got a dog? I've got Biscuit, cockapoo, he's a menace.
Craig: Staffy. Dexter. He's alright. Dodgy stomach.
Kerry: Oh no. Biscuit just eats shoes. Sixty quid trainers last week, I could've cried.
Craig: Dexter had a sausage roll off the floor. Up at three with him.
Kerry: Oh, gross. Right, well, I'd rather the trainers then.
Craig: Yeah. Probably.

=== CALL C0538 ===
Mark: Hiya, mate! Aneesa, is it? Did I say that right?
Aneesa: Yes, that's right. Hi. You're Mark?
Mark: Mark, yeah, Brierley Hill. Black Country. You're Bradford, ain't you? I saw the books in your photo and thought, she's way too clever for me, this one.
Aneesa: Ha. They're mostly novels. It's not that clever.
Mark: Novels! I ain't read a novel since school. Julie reads them, crime ones, on her phone. What do you do, then, are you at the university?
Aneesa: Sort of. I'm doing psychology with the Open University, part-time. And I work in a fragrance shop on Saturdays.
Mark: Psychology! So you're analysing me right now, are you?
Aneesa: A little bit. Only out of habit.
Mark: Go on then, what you got?
Aneesa: You're very relaxed for someone being filmed.
Mark: Ha! I am, yeah. Nothing to hide, me. I'm off work, back's gone, knee's gone. I just sit and talk to people. This is the most exciting thing I've done all week. Well, apart from the darts.
Aneesa: That's fair. I've done a few of these, actually. I like seeing how they're designed.
Mark: Designed, yeah? How do you mean?
Aneesa: Well, they had us rate photos first. Then we talk. Then the surveys after. I think they're checking whether you still like the people you thought you'd like. Or whether the photo was misleading.
Mark: Oh, that's crafty. So if I put someone down as a misery and they turn out sound, they've caught me out.
Aneesa: Basically, yeah.
Mark: Well I'll tell you now, I put you down as clever and you are clever, so I win.
Aneesa: Ha. Okay. What did you think of the puzzle?
Mark: Oh, don't. I was swearing at the laptop. Julie come in to check on me. I think I got about two right and one of them was a guess.
Aneesa: Most people guess the last few. It's probably meant to be hard.
Mark: That makes me feel better. Do you have to get up early for the shop, then?
Aneesa: Not that early. It's more being on my feet all day. I'm knackered by the time I get home, then I'm usually cooking tea.
Mark: Tea! Proper. Everyone down south says dinner. What do you cook?
Aneesa: Daal, karahi, keema. And sometimes Korean things off YouTube, which my brother and sister complain about and then eat anyway.
Mark: Ha! My grandkids are the same. Julie made a curry once, from a jar mind, my grandson said it was spicy and it had about as much spice as a custard cream.
Aneesa: That's a very Black Country description.
Mark: It is, ain't it? Slade are Black Country, you know. People think they're from Birmingham. They ain't.
Aneesa: I didn't know that. I'll keep it in mind if it comes up in a quiz.
Mark: It will, mate. It always does.

Aneesa: It was fine. I was more interested in why they put it first, to be honest. I think it's to put everyone in the same sort of mood before the calls. Or tired. One of the two.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah, I was tired after it. I'd just got in from work as well.
Aneesa: What do you do?
Rayhan: I'm an apprentice electrician, final year. Small firm in Barking, mostly houses: rewires, kitchens, bit of shop fit-out. I've got my AM2 coming up, that's like the final practical assessment, so I'm a bit... yeah. Revising for that.
Aneesa: That sounds quite intense. Is it all practical?
Rayhan: Mostly. You get a set time to install and test a little setup in a booth, and they mark everything. You can't really rush it. If you mess up the testing you're done, basically. I test twice anyway, the lads on site wind me up for it.
Aneesa: Twice seems sensible when it's electricity.
Rayhan: That's what I say! Erm, what about you, what do you do?
Aneesa: I'm doing a psychology degree with the Open University, second year. And I work part-time in a fragrance shop in town, Saturdays mainly.
Rayhan: Oh, nice. So is this sort of your area, then, these studies?
Aneesa: Kind of. I do a few of them. Partly for the money, I won't lie. But I like seeing how they're set up, what they're actually measuring. Like the photo bit earlier, rating people on a picture, that's a first impressions thing. Then they'll compare it with what we say after.
Rayhan: Oh. I didn't really think about that. I just sort of went with my gut.
Aneesa: That's what they want, I think. It's fine.
Rayhan: Yeah. Your photo, the planner on the wall, it reminded me of my sister. She's doing her GCSEs, she's got colours for every subject.
Aneesa: Guilty. Mine's colour-coded too. I've got a sister who's fourteen. She just borrows my eyeliner and ignores the planner entirely.
Rayhan: Ha. Mine's alright, she asks me for maths help. I got a 7 in maths so I'm the go-to.
Aneesa: That's useful. Do you get much time, with the work and revising?
Rayhan: Not loads. I do football Thursday, gym some mornings. Weekends is mostly family stuff, weddings. There's always a wedding.
Aneesa: There's always a wedding. Same here.
Rayhan: Have you been anywhere nice, travelling? I went to Istanbul last summer with two mates, first time without family.
Aneesa: Istanbul? That's the one place I really want to go. I'm learning Turkish on Duolingo, I've got a streak of four hundred and something days. Was it good?
Rayhan: It was really good, yeah. The mosques, like the Blue Mosque and Süleymaniye, the architecture is unbelievable. And the food. I did the whole itinerary in a spreadsheet, my mates took the mick but we saw everything.
Aneesa: You did a spreadsheet? I did that for Barcelona with my cousins. Every hour planned. They complained the whole time and then thanked me after.
Rayhan: Same! That's exactly what happened. Would you use the Turkish, if you went?
Aneesa: I'd try. I can order tea and ask where the toilet is, so I'd survive. I'd mostly want to sit in Süleymaniye and draw the tiles. I do geometric patterns, ink drawings.
Rayhan: Oh, is that the one behind you? The star?
Aneesa: Yeah, that's one of mine.
Rayhan: That's really neat. Like, properly precise. I'd mess that up.
Aneesa: You'd probably be fine. You test everything twice.
calls.C0534:
Kerry: Hiya! Oh, you're the West Brom shirt. I clocked that in the photos, I was like, he looks like a laugh.
Mark: Ha, guilty, mate. Mark. Brierley Hill. And you're, er, Kerry, is it?
Kerry: Kerry, yeah. Swindon. Don't say anything about the Magic Roundabout, everyone does.
Mark: I wasn't going to! I was, actually. Is it as bad as they say?
Kerry: Honestly, it's fine once you know it. It's the A419 that's the nightmare. I'm on it every day for work and it's just, do you know what I mean, cones for the sake of cones.
Mark: Oh, don't. Round Merry Hill they've had the road up that long, I reckon the cones have got their own postcode. What is it you do, then?
Kerry: Business development for a building and roofing supplier. So trade accounts, contractors, chasing new business across Wiltshire and Gloucestershire. Basically I'm the one who gets the big accounts in. It's a lot of phone, bit of site visits, showroom. I'm good at it, to be fair, I just think they don't pay what it's worth.
Mark: Nobody ever does, do they. Sounds like you can talk, anyway.
Kerry: I can talk, yeah. Did a negotiation skills course last year and the bloke running it said I was a natural. So.
Mark: There you go then. I'd have been rubbish at that, I just chat. I was on a depot, picking and loading, but the back went, so I'm off now. Just had a lad on before you, Craig, same thing, back's gone. We was swapping notes like two old crocks.
Kerry: Oh no. My back's not great either, to be honest, it's why I don't really do the gym. That's my excuse anyway.
Mark: That's a good excuse, I'd keep that one.
Kerry: Ha! I've had three memberships. Dan, my husband, says I just pay them a direct debit to feel guilty.
Mark: Julie says the same about my darts. I'm on the team down the local, Thursdays. She says it's not a sport if you can do it with a pint in your hand.
Kerry: She's not wrong though, is she?
Mark: She is not, no.
Kerry: Have you been watching The Traitors? Everyone at work's obsessed.
Mark: Julie has it on. I sort of half watch it with my tea and then ask who's who and she gets the hump.
Kerry: Oh, I'd get the hump. Last night was unreal. I'd be so good on that, I can read people, it's literally my job. I'd be a traitor, obviously.
Mark: Obviously! I'd be banished first week, me, I can't keep me face straight.
Kerry: You've got an honest face, to be fair.
Mark: That's what the darts lads say before I take their money. Got any kids, Kerry?
Kerry: Erm, no. No. We've got Biscuit, he's a cockapoo, he's basically the kid. He chewed my new trainers last week, sixty quid.
Mark: Oh, they do, don't they. My Roxy's too old to chew now, she just snores. I've got two grown up, and the grandkids. Off to Towyn with them next weekend in the caravan.
Kerry: Aw, Towyn. I couldn't do a caravan, I'm more all-inclusive, Tenerife, Turkey. Went to Dubai a couple of years ago, that was something else.
Mark: Dubai, eh? Bit posh for me, mate. Give me a pint by a pool in Benidorm and I'm happy.
Kerry: Nothing wrong with that. Bit of sun, cocktail, done.
Mark: Exactly, that's all you want, ain't it. Life's too short.
Kerry: It is. That's what I keep telling Dan when he looks at the bank statements.
Mark: Ha! Julie does the statements in our house. I'm not allowed near.
Kerry: Probably for the best, honestly.
calls.C0535:
Kerry: Hiya! You're the quiet lad with the hi-vis in the wardrobe. I'm Kerry, Swindon.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah, that's me. Rayhan. I'm in Ilford, East London.
Kerry: So are you on a site, then? Building?
Rayhan: Erm, sort of. I'm an apprentice electrician, final year. Mostly houses, rewires, kitchens, extensions. Bit of shop fit-out sometimes.
Kerry: No way! My husband's a sparky. Dan. Self-employed, round Swindon. So I know all about it, believe me. The van takes up the whole drive, there's cable in my kitchen drawers.
Rayhan: Ha, that sounds about right. My boss's van is the same, except it's always on empty.
Kerry: Oh, Dan's is always on empty and all. What is it with electricians? Are you going self-employed, then, when you're done?
Rayhan: Eventually, yeah, I'd like to. I've got my AM2 first, that's the final assessment. Then inspection and testing. Maybe my own van in my mid-twenties, me and a mate.
Kerry: Right. Well, honestly, do it. Dan's doing alright and he's terrible at the business side. Like he's a brilliant electrician, but quotes, invoices, chasing people for money, he's useless. I sort of do all that for him, or I tell him how to word things. That's literally my job, I'm business development for a building and roofing supplier. I sit on the phone and get contractors to open accounts with us. You want someone like me on your side when you go out on your own, do you know what I mean?
Rayhan: Yeah, that makes sense. I'm alright with the paperwork side, I keep my job notes and test sheets neat. It's more like getting customers that worries me.
Kerry: That's the easy bit! You just ring people. Find out who signs off the money and talk to them, not the receptionist. Don't waste your time being nice to the wrong person.
Rayhan: Erm, okay. I'd probably still be nice to the receptionist though.
Kerry: Ha. Fair enough, you're sweet. Where do you get your stuff from, Screwfix?
Rayhan: Mostly, yeah. Or the wholesaler the firm uses. The tool prices at Screwfix are mad, though.
Kerry: See, that's where a trade account comes in. You get the discounts. I do Dan's discounts, he never even asks, he just pays what's on the shelf.
Rayhan: Yeah, my boss has got one. I just use his.
Kerry: Use his while you can, mate. So what do you do when you're not wiring things?
Rayhan: Football Thursday, five-a-side. Gym some mornings. Watch Arsenal. Family stuff at weekends, there's always a wedding or something.
Kerry: Oh, I love a wedding. We had ours near Marlborough, big do at a hotel, honestly better than anyone else's I've been to. Free bar till ten.
Rayhan: That sounds nice.
Kerry: It was. Are you seeing anyone, then? Are they on at you about getting married?
Rayhan: Erm. A bit, yeah. My brother got married last year, so now everyone's looking at me. I'm not ready, I want to qualify first.
Kerry: Good for you. Don't let them rush you. Everyone's always asking me when I'm having kids, I'm like, mind your own.
Rayhan: Yeah. That's it really.
Kerry: Did you do that puzzle at the start? I thought it was a bit pointless, to be honest.
Rayhan: Erm, I didn't mind it. I was tired, I'd just come in from work.
Kerry: Oh, I'm knackered and all, I've been on the phone all day. Right, well, when you get your van, look me up. Swindon's not that far.
Rayhan: Ha, yeah. Thanks. I'll remember that.
calls.C0536:
Aneesa: Hi. Can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah, er, yeah. Hi. I'm Craig.
Aneesa: Aneesa. I'm in Bradford.
Craig: Lowestoft. Suffolk.
Aneesa: Is that the one right on the coast?
Craig: Yeah. Most easterly bit of the country, so. That's what it's known for really.

Craig: Staffy. Dexter. He's a bit chunky.
Aneesa: We don't have a dog. My brother keeps asking but my mum says no. He's seventeen, he'd never walk it.
Craig: Ha. No, probably not. It's sort of mostly me with Dexter. My wife works shifts.
Aneesa: What do you do?
Craig: Er... nothing at the minute. I was a welder. Offshore yard. Got laid off, then the back went. So I'm looking for something lighter.
Aneesa: Sorry, that sounds difficult.
Craig: Yeah. It's alright. It is what it is. You?
Aneesa: I'm doing a psychology degree, part-time, with the Open University. And I work in a fragrance shop on Saturdays.
Craig: Oh right. Psychology. So you're like, working out what this is all about, then? The study?
Aneesa: Ha, a bit. I can't help it. I think the photo ratings are the main thing, first impressions, and then these calls test whether you change your mind. And the surveys after, obviously.
Craig: Right. I just put whatever, to be honest.
Aneesa: That's fine. That's probably more useful to them than me overthinking it.
Craig: Ha. Yeah.
Aneesa: Is welding hard to learn? I've always wondered. It looks very precise.
Craig: Erm, it's practice really. MIG's easier, stick takes longer to get right. You've got to keep a steady hand and watch your pool, the molten bit. Get the speed wrong and it's all lumpy. I watch loads of videos of people doing it still, rebuilding old trailers and that. Saw one last week, bloke took this trailer that was basically rust and cut it all back, new box section, welded it up lovely. I could watch that all day.

Craig: Yeah, that's it. Is that the one behind you?
Aneesa: Yeah.
Craig: That's tidy, that.
Aneesa: Thank you. Do you still do any welding? Just for yourself?
Craig: Not really. I've got a motorbike in the yard, a 125, I'm meant to be doing it up. Been two years.
Aneesa: Two years? What's stopping you?
Craig: Dunno. I just go out and look at it. Bloke I had on earlier, Mark, he's got a car in his garage the same. He said we should start a club.
Aneesa: Ha. You'd need a planner. I'd make you one, colour-coded.
Craig: Ha. Yeah, Gemma'd love that. Yeah, it's alright, actually. Might do a bit this weekend.
calls.C0537:
Kerry: Hiya! You're Craig, yeah? I'm Kerry, Swindon. You remind me of my husband, by the way, that's a compliment.

calls.C0538:
Mark: Hiya, mate! Aneesa, is it? Did I say that right?
Aneesa: Yes, that's right. Hi. You're Mark?
Mark: Mark, yeah, Brierley Hill. Black Country. You're Bradford, ain't you? I saw the books in your photo and thought, she's way too clever for me, this one.
Aneesa: Ha. They're mostly novels. It's not that clever.
Mark: Novels! I ain't read a novel since school. Julie reads them, crime ones, on her phone. What do you do, then, are you at the university?
Aneesa: Sort of. I'm doing psychology with the Open University, part-time. And I work in a fragrance shop on Saturdays.
Mark: Psychology! So you're analysing me right now, are you?
Aneesa: A little bit. Only out of habit.
Mark: Go on then, what you got?
Aneesa: You're very relaxed for someone being filmed.
Mark: Ha! I am, yeah. Nothing to hide, me. I'm off work, back's gone, knee's gone. I just sit and talk to people. This is the most exciting thing I've done all week. Well, apart from the darts.
Aneesa: That's fair. I've done a few of these, actually. I like seeing how they're designed.
Mark: Designed, yeah? How do you mean?
Aneesa: Well, they had us rate photos first. Then we talk. Then the surveys after. I think they're checking whether you still like the people you thought you'd like. Or whether the photo was misleading.
Mark: Oh, that's crafty. So if I put someone down as a misery and they turn out sound, they've caught me out.
Aneesa: Basically, yeah.
Mark: Well I'll tell you now, I put you down as clever and you are clever, so I win.
Aneesa: Ha. Okay. What did you think of the puzzle?
Mark: Oh, don't. I was swearing at the laptop. Julie come in to check on me. I think I got about two right and one of them was a guess.
Aneesa: Most people guess the last few. It's probably meant to be hard.
Mark: That makes me feel better. Do you have to get up early for the shop, then?
Aneesa: Not that early. It's more being on my feet all day. I'm knackered by the time I get home, then I'm usually cooking tea.
Mark: Tea! Proper. Everyone down south says dinner. What do you cook?
Aneesa: Daal, karahi, keema. And sometimes Korean things off YouTube, which my brother and sister complain about and then eat anyway.
Mark: Ha! My grandkids are the same. Julie made a curry once, from a jar mind, my grandson said it was spicy and it had about as much spice as a custard cream.
Aneesa: That's a very Black Country description.
Mark: It is, ain't it? Slade are Black Country, you know. People think they're from Birmingham. They ain't.
Aneesa: I didn't know that. I'll keep it in mind if it comes up in a quiz.
Mark: It will, mate. It always does.

C0532.line_text: I know how that feels, mate, honestly. First year I was off I felt proper useless. You get used to it. Not saying it's right, but you do. What you looking at doing, then, anything?
C0532.what: Mark's grin drops and he looks down and away from the camera for a few seconds, rubbing his stubble, before looking back at the screen and carrying on.
